children: The European Union's executive arm outlined a plan to revamp public bidding across its 27 member states that will empower them to exclude some foreign bidders under certain circumstances.

The proposals announced on Wednesday seek to make the EU's public bidding processes easier for companies to follow and boost investments. They will also allow public authorities to leave out companies from countries that don't provide reciprocal access to European firms, which could raise scrutiny for bidders from markets like China.

It is the latest move from EU officials in recent months to use the bloc's public funding toolkit to help drive demand for European companies and boost their growth and competitiveness. The EU's industry commissioner Stephane Sejourne told reporters on Wednesday that public procurement makes up around 15% of Europe's GDP.

Under the plan, the European Commission wants to unify other pieces of legislation on procurement into one legal text to reduce their complexity and inconsistencies on how they are applied across different sectors such as transport and energy. A second proposal focuses on investments into local companies for research and development.
"We're doing away with decades of built-up complexity, complaints received by public authorities, challenges faced by businesses when trying to respond to the calls for tender," Sejourne said.
EU lawmakers and member states will have to negotiate on the rulebooks--officially named the Public Procurement Act and European Innovation Act--before they can come into effect.

Under the rules, public bodies would be encouraged to seek out European goods and services in public contracts without mandating quotas. It also aims to clarify to public buyers how they select bids and encourages them to put more focus on factors such as sustainability and quality instead of just the price they offer.

Contracts, the proposal said, should "be awarded on the basis of the best price-quality ratio", with factors such as innovation and resilience to account for at least 30% of a winning bid's value, rising to 50% for labour-intensive contracts.

Public buyers will also be able to exclude bids coming from non-EU countries--such as China--that don't provide similar access to EU firms if they wish to. The commission's proposal cites the World Trade Organization's Agreement on Government  Procurement, which essentially facilitates international competition for public contracts between the countries and regions that are party to it. The EU, the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Japan and Singapore are bound to that agreement, while China is not.

The innovation rulebook--which is also geared towards addressing fragmentation in the EU and helping to scale up ideas--would ask public buyers to focus on companies within Europe for precommercial research and development projects.

Responding to the proposal on Wednesday, China's Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it is "highly concerned" about its provisions on European preference, market access for other countries and supply chain security. "We are strongly opposed to any measures that would exclude or restrict third-country companies from participating in EU public procurement on the basis of so-called non-market factors," the group said.
